scope: Two Euclidean remainder steps halve the denominator. Starting below 2^k, the algorithm performs at most 2k divisions.

Identifies termination of the real continued fraction for a measured rational o/Q with an explicit Euclidean division count. The scan over the first 2(log₂ Q + 1) + 1 indices suffices for every o < Q, with the logarithm rounded down.
The explicit logarithmic scan satisfies ForShor’s continued-fraction completeness specification for every clock width.

The ideal initialized Fourier circuit and the bounded order decoder together return the exact order with Born probability at least 4φ(r)/(π²r), hence at least φ(r)/(3r). ForShor chooses N² < Q ≤ 2N². This includes the paper’s clock for moduli which are not powers of two.
After ceil(12 ln(1+floor(log₂(r+1)))) independent trials, the failure bound obtained from the φ(r)/(3r) certificate is at most exp(−1).

Finite matrix semantics of the reference two-limb Toom–Cook implementation. On the all-zero input, at precision chosen for the modulus and with fqchem’s bounded decoder, its one-run success probability is at least a strictly positive certified bound.
The checked interpolation table gives an admissible constant lowering policy for the modular arithmetic circuit.
The submitted low-level circuit achieves the reference bound using its allocated layout, selected precision, all-zero input, and any complete continued-fraction scan.
There is enough precision for the reference circuit to receive a positive probability certificate at every modulus.
An explicit lower bound for the unit fraction φ(r)/r, logarithmic in the bit width, supplies the independent-retry estimate.
Preparing the zero registers and applying Hadamards and modular exponentiation yields the pre-inverse-QFT state used in Section 5.
There are at least φ(r) distinct good clock outcomes and each has probability at least 4/(π²r). Summation gives the order-recovery mass.
For the initialized ideal circuit the Born distribution agrees with the finite exponential sums of Section 5.
The register bounds imply r² < Q and every good outcome passes the order check within a complete scan.
For a circuit within its qubit ceiling, the abstract Born probability on zero input equals the finite-dimensional circuit matrix probability.
An executable positive-denominator scan using binary modular multiplication returns exactly the same natural number as ForShor’s specification.
At the explicit integer precision schedule the number of extra modular work bits is bounded by 70 times the data width.

For the two-limb reference multiplication table and explicit precision level, the same circuit evaluated by programRecovery uses O(n³) logical gates at data width n, in the ForShor elementary-gate model.
The explicit two-limb circuit on the zero vector, measured in its finite matrix semantics, has success at least 1/(2π² ln(1+floor(log₂ N))). Its executable decoder and precision schedule are fixed.
The executable precision level 2²⁶n⁴ gives enough accuracy for the lowered circuit to keep half the ideal success certificate.
Summation of Born weights over clock outcomes returning a verified factor gives a nonnegative result.
For each good unit the circuit’s exact-order outcomes yield genuine factors after the executable gcd check. Thus the one-shot factor probability is at least the quantum recovery certificate.
Every clock outcome of the physical low-level matrix circuit has nonnegative Born weight.
Averaging the physical matrix Born probability over a uniformly chosen unit proves an unconditional one-run lower bound (1−2^(1−k))/(2π² ln(1+floor(log₂ N))) for odd N>1 with k distinct primes.
Converting the chosen unit to the input structure preserves the multiplicative order used by the quantum circuit.
Computes the extra register bits at an integer reference precision in terms of the natural ceiling logarithm.
The reference allocator sets the data register width to floor(log₂(2N)).
The reference allocator sets the clock width to floor(log₂(2N²)).
At sufficiently fine approximation precision the complete lowered circuit keeps half the reference success bound.
An admissible Toom–Cook interpolation table with bounded exponent gives the logical gate-count bound for all ready layouts and linearly many extra work bits.
The constant 1/π² in the compiled success bound is positive.
The reciprocal precision needed for a valid order-finding layout grows at most quartically with data width.
An initialized ready layout supplies the workspace required by the compiler.
Taking the least nonzero executable candidate returns the true order whenever at least one trial recovers it. Every positive candidate passes modular verification and hence is at least the order.

At Shor’s binary clock, the wrong-answer probability of the independent Fourier experiments and bounded decoder is ≤1/e in ceil(12 ln(1+floor(log₂(r+1)))) trials. The joint law is the product of the normalized matrix Born distributions.
Each clock outcome has nonnegative weight in the explicit projected matrix column.
Summing over the complete clock register gives probability one. The circuit matrix is unitary, the input is the zero basis vector, and the register projectors partition the final amplitudes.
For an arbitrary positive base, the stochastic output measure counts exactly the verified factor probability, including the immediate gcd branch.
For any composite m ≤ N, preprocessing and one fair-word trial return a checked proper divisor with probability at least 1/[128(1+floor(log₂ N))].
Summation over uniformly sampled fair words accounts for rejected draws; one physical trial keeps at least half the mean accepted-base factor probability.
Two order-finding inputs with the same base and modulus describe the same quantum experiment.

The finite-matrix circuit, bit decoder, classical gcd check and recursive splitter return primes multiplying to N with probability at least 2/3. The product is exact on every tape and the bound on trial count is cubic in the input bit length.
Every accepted factor in the pushed-forward clock distribution satisfies both strict bounds and divides the modulus.
Pushing the normalized clock measure through the executable decoder and factor extractor recovers its explicit finite Born sum.
The fair-word sample space has between N−1 and 2(N−1) elements, so at least half the words encode usable positive bases.
Whenever the verified extractor accepts the true order, every circuit outcome decoding that order returns the certified divisor.

A uniform draw from all integers 1,…,N−1 and one compiled experiment yield a factor with probability at least (1−2^(1−k))/(2π² ln(1+floor(log₂ N))). This includes nonunits, for which the first gcd already splits N.
Converting a positive coprime base less than N to a modular unit preserves its natural representative.
Every Fourier phase has unit modulus, as needed for normalization of the clock transform.
An interval-allocated register has exactly its declared binary width.
Every positive exponent passing modular verification is at least the multiplicative order.
A near-peak outcome for an index coprime to the order passes the complete continued-fraction decoder.
The finite matrix of the lowered circuit is unitary at every qubit dimension large enough for its gates.
The register projector keeps exactly the amplitudes whose measured bits encode the requested outcome.
The integer obtained by reading the register bits is smaller than the register basis size.
